title: Book 02 — Chapter 1: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 1: ‘Ali’s Struggles
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Questions were checked against the original Al-Islam.org chapter. The answers distinguish the author's historical narrative, analysis of the Kharijites, and lessons about justice, political honesty, religious training, and responsible verification of claims.

revision_policy: Exam-ready answers with clear reasoning and source traceability.
Distinguish the political use of religious symbols from genuine religious commitment.
Explain the Kharijites through the source's emphasis on outward devotion without knowledge and insight.
Preserve the Imam’s distinction between tolerating dissent and confronting armed violence.
Do not omit the chapter’s lesson about verifying reports before repeating accusations.

questions.prompt: Why did Imam ‘Ali initially hesitate when people urged him to accept the caliphate after ‘Uthman’s assassination?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Imam ‘Ali did not hesitate because he considered himself unworthy of the caliphate. He foresaw that the political situation was deeply chaotic and that the problems awaiting him had many sides and no clear solution. The revolutionaries who had participated in ‘Uthman’s overthrow had gathered around him, but the wider Muslim community did not share a single view of the revolution or its demands. ‘Ali warned that if he accepted leadership, he would govern according to his own understanding of justice and not according to the expectations of those urging him to take power. He therefore said that he would rather remain a minister than become a chief unless people accepted the way he intended to lead.
questions.source_locator: Why did ‘Ali hesitate to accept the caliphate?

questions.prompt: What was the first major difficulty Imam ‘Ali inherited when he accepted the caliphate?
questions.answer: The first major difficulty was the assassination of ‘Uthman and the political turmoil surrounding it. The previous caliph had been killed in a revolution, and the rebels who had prevented his burial later joined the people pledging allegiance to ‘Ali. However, not everyone viewed the revolutionaries or their demands in the same way. ‘Ali’s own views did not fully match either the position of ‘Uthman’s supporters or that of the revolutionaries. He therefore inherited a government in which the killing of the previous caliph had already created deep divisions and a serious risk of further conflict.
questions.source_locator: ‘Uthman’s assassination — The problem of hypocrisy

questions.prompt: How did Mu‘awiyah use ‘Uthman’s assassination as a political weapon against Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Mu‘awiyah used the blood of ‘Uthman as a political instrument to turn public anger against ‘Ali. He had arranged for ‘Uthman’s blood-stained shirt and the fingers of ‘Uthman’s wife to be sent to Syria immediately after the assassination. He displayed them publicly, delivered emotional speeches about the murdered caliph, and accused ‘Ali of cooperating with the revolutionaries. Mutahhari questions Mu‘awiyah’s right to demand vengeance when ‘Uthman had closer relatives who were more directly entitled to seek it. The episode illustrates how Mu‘awiyah used a seemingly religious and moral cause to pursue his own political ambitions.
questions.source_locator: ‘Uthman’s assassination — The problem of hypocrisy

questions.prompt: Why did Imam ‘Ali refuse to continue the special financial privileges that influential people had received under earlier administrations?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that after the Prophet’s death, society had become accustomed to special subsidies and financial privileges for influential people. Imam ‘Ali refused to continue this practice because it violated justice and deprived weaker people of their rights. Even some of his followers advised him to show political flexibility so that he could secure victory and retain power. ‘Ali rejected the suggestion, asking whether political success should be purchased at the cost of oppression and the destruction of the rights of the powerless. He declared that he would not deviate from justice even slightly, regardless of the political consequences.
questions.source_locator: Inflexibility in the enforcement of justice

questions.prompt: What was the third major difficulty Mutahhari identifies in Imam ‘Ali’s political conduct?
questions.answer: The third difficulty was Imam ‘Ali’s honesty and refusal to use deception as a political tool. Some supporters argued that politics required manipulation, dishonesty, and cunning, and they compared ‘Ali unfavourably with Mu‘awiyah’s diplomacy. ‘Ali responded that Mu‘awiyah was not more intelligent or capable; he was simply deceitful. ‘Ali refused to stray from truth or commit immoral acts for political advantage. He regarded deception as wicked and as something for which a person would be accountable before God. Mutahhari presents this integrity as a political difficulty because some people expected the Imam to use the same methods as his opponents.
questions.source_locator: Bluntness and honesty in politics

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari identify as the main difference between the community trained by the Prophet and the society Imam ‘Ali had to govern?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Prophet did not simply gather large numbers of people under a banner. During the thirteen years in Mecca, he patiently trained a core group that understood Islam’s principles, objectives, and moral teachings. By the time of migration, this group was relatively small but had received deep Islamic education. Later conquests expanded the Muslim population, but teaching and training did not always keep pace with expansion. As a result, many people knew the outward forms of Islam but had not absorbed its inner meaning. Imam ‘Ali inherited a society containing this untrained group, which made his task much more difficult.
questions.source_locator: Kharijites — Why training must precede expansion

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari distinguish the opponents faced by the Prophet from those faced by Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Prophet’s opponents were predominantly open non-believers and idol-worshippers who rejected Islam openly. Their slogans and objectives were clear. Imam ‘Ali, however, faced opponents who presented themselves as Muslims and used Islamic slogans and Qur’anic language while pursuing aims contrary to Islam. Their opposition was therefore concealed beneath an appearance of piety. Mutahhari describes this as hypocrisy or covert paganism. The distinction made ‘Ali’s task more difficult because he had to expose people who appeared religious and could manipulate religious symbols against the Imam.
questions.source_locator: Kharijites — Why training must precede expansion

questions.prompt: Why did Mutahhari regard the Kharijites as a fundamental problem for Imam ‘Ali rather than merely another political opposition group?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that the Kharijites were dangerous because they combined intense outward religious observance with ignorance of the essence of Islam. They were devoted to prayer and fasting, yet lacked knowledge of the Qur’an’s meaning, the Prophet’s traditions, and the objectives of Islamic teachings. Their rigid beliefs led them to accuse other Muslims of disbelief and to justify violence against those who disagreed with them. They could be manipulated by politically skilled hypocrites such as Mu‘awiyah and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. The danger was therefore not only military opposition; it was a distorted religious mentality that could spread through the Muslim community.
questions.source_locator: Kharijites — Why training must precede expansion

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of raising copies of the Qur’an on spears during the Battle of Siffin?
questions.answer: When Mu‘awiyah’s forces realized that they were close to defeat, they raised copies of the Qur’an on spears and called for the Qur’an to judge between the two sides. The move appealed to the religious feelings of members of ‘Ali’s army, especially those who lacked deeper understanding of the conflict. They stopped fighting and demanded arbitration, even though ‘Ali had already called for the dispute to be judged according to the Qur’an. Mutahhari explains that the tactic used the outward symbol of the Qur’an to prevent its actual guidance from being applied and to rescue Mu‘awiyah from military defeat.
questions.source_locator: The Qur’ans-on-spears stratagem

questions.prompt: Why did Imam ‘Ali reject the Kharijites’ claim that arbitration was an act of disbelief or polytheism?
questions.answer: The Kharijites misinterpreted the Qur’anic statement that judgement belongs to God alone. They argued that no human beings could be appointed to resolve a dispute and that choosing arbitrators was therefore an act of disbelief. Imam ‘Ali explained that the law and ultimate authority belong to God, but human beings may be appointed to judge according to the Qur’an and the law God has revealed. The purpose of arbitration was not to create a new law or replace divine authority; it was to apply the Qur’anic law to the dispute. ‘Ali refused to confess to a sin he had not committed or to declare a legitimate procedure unlawful.
questions.source_locator: Arbitration and refusal to admit error

questions.prompt: How did Imam ‘Ali treat the Kharijites before they began armed rebellion?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam ‘Ali tolerated the Kharijites for a long time despite their insults and public opposition. He did not cut off their share of the public treasury or restrict their freedom merely because they disagreed with him. They heckled his sermons and even insulted him during public gatherings, yet he prevented his companions from retaliating violently. He also allowed them to pray separately and express their beliefs. ‘Ali only moved against them when they turned their opposition into an armed rebellion and began committing violence against other people.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali’s demeanour towards the Kharijites — Tolerating opposition before violence

questions.prompt: What were the main doctrinal principles of the Kharijites described by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Kharijites declared ‘Uthman, Imam ‘Ali, Mu‘awiyah, and those who accepted arbitration to be unbelievers, while claiming that only those who repented according to their own doctrine were Muslims. They treated enjoining good and forbidding evil as an unconditional duty that required people to rise against any ruler they considered unlawful, even when an uprising had no chance of success. They also held that committing a major sin made a person a non-believer and impure. These principles produced extreme exclusivism: they considered only their own group to be Muslim and treated everyone else as outside the faith.
questions.source_locator: The principles of the Kharijites sect

questions.prompt: What examples does Mutahhari give to show the violence produced by the Kharijites’ rigid beliefs?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes the Kharijites stopping a companion of the Prophet who was travelling with his pregnant wife. They demanded that he disown Imam ‘Ali. When he refused, they killed him and attacked his pregnant wife. He also recounts an incident in which a Kharijite picked up a date from a palm garden belonging to a respected Muslim, and his companions immediately rebuked him for taking another person’s property. Mutahhari uses these examples to expose the contradiction between their strictness about minor matters and their readiness to kill innocent people. Their religious rigidity did not produce justice or compassion; it produced violence and hypocrisy.
questions.source_locator: The principles of the Kharijites sect

questions.prompt: How did Imam ‘Ali resolve the crisis at Nahrawan, and what happened to the Kharijites who reconsidered their position?
questions.answer: Imam ‘Ali first sent Ibn ‘Abbas to speak with the Kharijites, but the discussion did not resolve the crisis. ‘Ali then went personally and addressed them. Mutahhari says that there were approximately twelve thousand people in the group; eight thousand were persuaded to reconsider their position and accepted the Imam’s protection banner. The remaining four thousand refused to return. ‘Ali then fought the armed group at Nahrawan. Only about ten survived, one of whom was ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, who later assassinated the Imam. The account illustrates that ‘Ali first attempted dialogue and reconciliation before using force against those who persisted in armed rebellion.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali’s attitude towards the Kharijites — Dialogue, protection, and Nahrawan

questions.prompt: What three characteristics of the Kharijites does Mutahhari identify?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies extraordinary bravery and devotion, excessive worship combined with dogmatism, and ignorance or lack of understanding of Islam. The Kharijites were not necessarily lazy or irreligious; they prayed for long periods and displayed intense commitment to their beliefs. Their problem was that their worship was not accompanied by sound knowledge, insight, or understanding of the objectives of Islam. Their rigidity and lack of knowledge made them vulnerable to manipulation and led them to accuse others of disbelief. Mutahhari’s point is that outward religious devotion alone does not guarantee correct understanding or moral judgement.
questions.source_locator: The distinguishing features of the Kharijites

questions.prompt: What lesson does Mutahhari draw from the story of the false accusation against Muhammad Iqbal?
questions.answer: Mutahhari recounts that someone accused Muhammad Iqbal of insulting Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq based on a passage that the accuser had not personally checked. The misunderstanding arose because Iqbal was referring to two Indian figures named Ja‘far and Sadiq who had betrayed Muslim resistance against the British, not to Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq. Mutahhari uses the incident to warn against spreading accusations based on hearsay. He urges people to investigate the original source, understand the context, and verify claims before repeating them. The story illustrates how ignorance and careless rumour can damage the reputation of scholars and divide the Muslim community.
questions.source_locator: The distinguishing features of the Kharijites — The Iqbal anecdote and unverified accusations

questions.prompt: What instructions did Imam ‘Ali give regarding the Kharijites after his own assassination?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam ‘Ali instructed his followers not to kill the Kharijites after his death. He distinguished between people who seek truth but make a mistake and those who deliberately seek falsehood. The Kharijites, in his judgement, were mistaken in their understanding even though their actions had become dangerous. He warned that killing them after his death would serve Mu‘awiyah’s interests rather than truth and justice. This instruction shows ‘Ali’s refusal to act out of personal revenge, even against those who had fought him and contributed to his death.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali’s martyrdom — His final instructions and the distinction between kinds of opponents

questions.prompt: Explain the major difficulties Imam ‘Ali faced during his caliphate and how they contributed to the crisis of his rule.
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies several interconnected difficulties. First, ‘Ali inherited the consequences of ‘Uthman’s assassination: the revolutionaries who had killed the previous caliph joined his supporters, while other Muslims held different views about the uprising. Mu‘awiyah exploited the murder as a political weapon and accused ‘Ali of responsibility. Second, ‘Ali refused to continue special financial privileges for influential people and insisted on justice, even when his followers urged political compromise. Third, he rejected deception and dishonesty as political tools, refusing to imitate Mu‘awiyah’s manipulation. Finally, he faced the Kharijites, a group whose outward piety concealed ignorance and rigid beliefs. Their religious slogans made them difficult to confront, and their actions threatened the unity and moral foundations of the Muslim community. Mutahhari presents these problems as a combination of political hypocrisy, social change, principled justice, and religious extremism.
questions.source_locator: Why did ‘Ali hesitate to accept the caliphate?

questions.prompt: How did Mu‘awiyah turn the assassination of ‘Uthman into a political campaign against Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Mu‘awiyah used the assassination of ‘Uthman as a means of mobilizing public anger against Imam ‘Ali. He had arranged for the blood-stained shirt of ‘Uthman and the fingers of ‘Uthman’s wife to be sent to Syria immediately after the murder. He displayed these items publicly and delivered emotional sermons portraying ‘Uthman as an innocent caliph whose blood had to be avenged. He then accused ‘Ali of cooperating with the revolutionaries because some of them had joined ‘Ali’s army. Mutahhari points out that Mu‘awiyah was a distant relative and that ‘Uthman had closer relatives who were more directly entitled to seek vengeance. The political purpose was to turn a real tragedy into a pretext for war against ‘Ali, contributing to the conflicts of Jamal and Siffin.
questions.source_locator: ‘Uthman’s assassination — The problem of hypocrisy

questions.prompt: Explain how Imam ‘Ali’s commitment to justice and honesty created political difficulties for him.
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that Imam ‘Ali refused to sacrifice justice for political success. Society had become accustomed to giving special financial privileges to influential people, but ‘Ali refused to continue those arrangements because they deprived the weak of their rights. Even his own supporters urged him to be flexible, but he insisted that victory purchased through oppression was unacceptable. In politics, he also refused to use deception, manipulation, or dishonesty, even when people praised Mu‘awiyah for his apparent diplomacy. ‘Ali explained that Mu‘awiyah was not more intelligent but more deceitful, and he would not commit immoral acts to gain power. These principles made it difficult for ‘Ali to compete in a political environment where opponents used bribery, propaganda, and manipulation. Mutahhari presents his difficulties as the cost of remaining faithful to justice and truth.
questions.source_locator: Inflexibility in the enforcement of justice

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari argue that the Prophet’s method of training a committed core group was essential, and how did neglecting that method contribute to the rise of the Kharijites?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Prophet did not simply gather large numbers of people under a political banner. During the thirteen years in Mecca, he patiently taught and trained a core group that understood Islam’s principles, objectives, and moral spirit. By the time of migration, this group was relatively small but deeply educated in the essence of Islam. Later Muslim conquests expanded the community, but the process of teaching and training did not keep pace. Many new Muslims learned the outward forms of prayer and worship without understanding the purposes and principles behind them. This created a group that was intensely observant but lacked insight and knowledge. The Kharijites emerged from this environment: they displayed excessive worship and strictness but misunderstood the Qur’an, declared other Muslims unbelievers, and used religious language to justify violence. Mutahhari’s central lesson is that expansion without education and moral training can produce a community vulnerable to extremism and manipulation.
questions.source_locator: Kharijites — Why training must precede expansion

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the events of the Qur’an-on-spears stratagem and explain why the Kharijites later accused Imam ‘Ali of disbelief for accepting arbitration.
questions.answer: At Siffin, Mu‘awiyah’s forces were close to defeat when they raised copies of the Qur’an on spears and called for the Qur’an to judge between the two sides. Some members of ‘Ali’s army, who did not understand the political manoeuvre, stopped fighting and pressured the Imam to accept arbitration. ‘Ali warned that the enemy was using the covers and pages of the Qur’an as a tactic, but his soldiers threatened him and demanded that Malik al-Ashtar return from the battlefield. Under this pressure, ‘Ali accepted arbitration. When the process was manipulated by ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, the Kharijites claimed that choosing human arbitrators violated the Qur’anic statement that judgement belongs to God alone. ‘Ali explained that the law belongs to God, but people may be appointed to judge according to the Qur’an. He refused to confess to a sin he had not committed. Mutahhari uses the episode to show how shallow religious literalism can be exploited by political deception and can turn against the very Imam who is defending the Qur’an.
questions.source_locator: The Qur’ans-on-spears stratagem

questions.prompt: How did Imam ‘Ali distinguish between tolerating the Kharijites’ beliefs and responding to their armed violence?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Imam ‘Ali tolerated the Kharijites for as long as their opposition remained verbal and non-violent. He did not stop their share of the public treasury, restrict their freedom, or prevent them from expressing their beliefs. Even when they insulted him during sermons or accused him of disbelief during prayer, he restrained his companions from retaliating. However, when the Kharijites formed an armed rebellion, began robbing and killing people, and attacked innocent Muslims, the situation changed. ‘Ali first sent Ibn ‘Abbas to speak with them and then went personally to persuade them. Eight thousand of the twelve thousand reportedly accepted his protection, while the remaining armed group was confronted at Nahrawan. The distinction is between allowing dissent and permitting violence against the community. Mutahhari presents ‘Ali as patient toward disagreement but firm against armed aggression.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali’s demeanour towards the Kharijites — Tolerating opposition before violence

questions.prompt: Describe the Kharijites’ doctrine and explain how it transformed religious devotion into extremism and violence.
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Kharijites developed rigid doctrines that treated ‘Uthman, ‘Ali, Mu‘awiyah, and those who accepted arbitration as unbelievers. They claimed that only those who repented according to their own principles were Muslims. They also held that committing a major sin made a person a non-believer and impure, and that enjoining good and forbidding evil required an uprising against any ruler they considered unlawful, even if the uprising had no prospect of success. These beliefs produced extreme exclusivism: they treated other Muslims as outside the faith and considered violence against them permissible. Mutahhari illustrates the result through the murder of a Prophet’s companion and his pregnant wife, as well as the Kharijites’ strict reaction to a member who took a single date from another person’s garden. The contrast shows that outward piety and strictness can coexist with ignorance, injustice, and cruelty when they are not guided by knowledge and sound understanding.
questions.source_locator: The principles of the Kharijites sect

questions.prompt: Explain the circumstances of Imam ‘Ali’s assassination, his final instructions, and why his burial place was kept secret.
questions.answer: Mutahhari recounts that ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, one of a group of ascetic extremists who blamed ‘Ali, Mu‘awiyah, and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As for the turmoil in the Muslim world, was selected to assassinate the Imam. The attack was planned for the night before the nineteenth of Ramadan, which the conspirators regarded as a night of great worship. Ibn Muljam’s relationship with Qutam, a Kharijite woman, became part of the plot, and she demanded the killing of ‘Ali as part of her dowry. After the attack, ‘Ali instructed his followers not to kill the Kharijites after his death, distinguishing those who seek truth but err from those who deliberately pursue falsehood. He was brought before Ibn Muljam and questioned him without personal vengeance. ‘Ali died on the night of the twenty-first of Ramadan. His children and a small group of followers washed and buried him secretly because they feared the Kharijites would desecrate his grave. The location remained concealed for about a century until Imam al-Sadiq later revealed it.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali’s martyrdom — Ibn Muljam, Qutam, and the assassination plot
